title: Props and Component Communication
subtitle: Make Your Components Dynamic - One Card, 10 Different Lessons
description: Master props, props destructuring, default props, children props, prop drilling, and how parent-child communication makes your dashboard scalable. Build dynamic LessonCards that render from data.

blocks.text: PAGE 1: The Problem - Why Your Dashboard Needs Props

Hey! Look at your dashboard code you gave me. You have 10 lessons defined in an array, but you don't want to write 10 different LessonCard components, right? Imagine: LessonCard1, LessonCard2... LessonCard10 - copy paste 10 times! If you want to change design, you change 10 files. Nightmare!

Props solve this. Props = Properties. Think of components as functions. In normal functions you pass arguments: add(2,3). In React components you pass props: <LessonCard title="React Hooks" status="current" />. Same component, different data, different UI.
Today's target: Make your LessonCard dynamic so it can show Lesson 1, 2, 3... 10 from data. This is exactly how your dashboard will work in Lesson 10 final project.
Quick task: Open Menu > Practical > React editor now. Keep it open - we will build live together every page.
PAGE 2: What Are Props? The Real-Life Analogy

Imagine you order a shirt online. You choose: size=M, color=Blue, text='Code Academy'. The shirt factory is the Component, your choices are Props. Factory makes same shirt design but with YOUR props. Different props = different shirt, same factory.
In React: Component = Shirt Factory. Props = Your choices. You call <Shirt size="M" color="blue" />. Component receives props object: {size: "M", color: "blue"} and builds UI accordingly.

Key rules: 1. Props flow DOWN from parent to child only (unidirectional). 2. Props are READ-ONLY - child cannot change props, only parent can. 3. Props can be anything: string, number, array, object, function, even another component!

blocks.question: APPLICATION: You have a Button component. You want one button to say 'Start Lesson' and another to say 'Locked'. How do you do it with props?
options: Create two different components: StartButton and LockedButton
Create one Button component with prop: <Button text="Start Lesson" /> and <Button text="Locked" />

blocks.incorrectFeedback: Think shirt factory analogy - same factory, different text prop. <Button text="Start Lesson" /> vs <Button text="Locked" />
blocks.reasoning: Props enable reusability - core React pattern.

PAGE 4: Destructuring Props - Clean Code Pro Way

Writing props.title, props.learn, props.status every time is tiring. Pro developers destructure: function LessonCard({ id, title, learn, status }) - directly extract what you need. Same result, cleaner code.

blocks.question: APPLICATION: Your designer says LessonCard should show status badge color: green for completed, blue for current, gray for locked. How would props help?
options: Hardcode green color always
Pass status prop and use conditional inside component: {status==='completed'? green : status==='current'? blue : gray}
Create 3 separate CSS files
Props cannot control colors
blocks.correctFeedback: Exactly! Props + conditional rendering = dynamic colors. This is exactly how your dashboard badge colors work.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Use prop to decide color: status prop tells component which color to show. Same component, different colors based on props.
blocks.reasoning: Props drive conditional UI - essential for real dashboards.

blocks.text: PAGE 5: Default Props - What If Parent Forgets to Pass Prop?

What if you render <LessonCard title="React Hooks" /> but forget status? Then props.status is undefined, UI breaks. Default props give fallback: function LessonCard({ status = "locked" }) - if parent doesn't pass status, use "locked" as default. Your dashboard should default to locked for safety!

blocks.text: PAGE 6: Children Prop - The Special Prop

Children is a special prop. Whatever you put BETWEEN opening and closing tag becomes props.children. Example:

Hello

is children of Card. This is how you make wrapper components like your hero, card, layout.

blocks.title: Example 5: Children Prop - Wrapper Components

blocks.question: APPLICATION: You want a <Layout> component that shows Navbar at top, whatever content you put inside in middle, Footer at bottom. Which prop helps?
options: Use props.children - <Layout><MyPage /></Layout> and inside Layout render {children} between Navbar and Footer
You need 3 different layouts
Children prop doesn't exist in React
Use props.title only
blocks.correctFeedback: Perfect! Children prop is for layout wrappers - Navbar + {children} + Footer pattern used by every real app.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Children prop: Whatever between tags becomes children. Layout uses it to wrap any page content.
blocks.reasoning: Children prop enables composition and layout patterns.

blocks.text: PAGE 7: Props Are Read-Only - The Golden Rule

Never do props.title = "New Title" inside child. Props are immutable, read-only. Why? If child changes props, parent doesn't know, data flow breaks, bugs everywhere. It's like child changing parent's shirt order without telling parent. Rule: Child can READ props, only parent can CHANGE props by passing new props.

blocks.question: APPLICATION: You have 100 products from API. You need to show ProductCard for each. What's the efficient React way?
options: Write <ProductCard /> 100 times manually
Create one ProductCard with props and do products.map(product => <ProductCard key={product.id} {...product} />)
You cannot show 100 products in React
Use HTML table only
blocks.correctFeedback: YES! Map + props + key - that's how real e-commerce sites like Jumia show products. One component, 100 different data.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Don't copy paste 100 times. Use map() to loop data and pass props to one ProductCard component.
blocks.reasoning: List rendering with props is fundamental for real applications.

blocks.text: PAGE 9: Props Drilling - Passing Props Down Multiple Levels

What if App has user name, but Header is inside Navbar which is inside App, and UserAvatar is inside Header? You need to pass prop through: App -> Navbar -> Header -> UserAvatar. This chain is called Prop Drilling. It works but can get annoying if chain is long. In Lesson 9 we will learn better ways (Context API), but for now, drilling is okay and you must understand it.

blocks.text: PAGE 10: Props Can Be Functions - Child Talks Back to Parent!

Wait, I said props flow down only, how can child talk back? Trick: Parent passes a FUNCTION as prop. Child calls that function when something happens. Parent's function runs. So child can notify parent! This is crucial for Lesson 4 (state) and Lesson 6 (forms).

blocks.question: APPLICATION: In your dashboard, when user clicks 'Start Lesson' button inside LessonCard, you want to navigate to that lesson's page. How?
options: LessonCard should directly change window.location by itself without props
App passes a function prop onStart to LessonCard, LessonCard calls onStart when button clicked, App handles navigation
You cannot navigate from child component
Props cannot be functions
blocks.correctFeedback: Perfect! That's the pattern - parent passes function as prop, child calls it on event. This is how your backBtn and lesson navigation will work!
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Pass function as prop: Parent gives child a function like onStart, child calls it on button click to notify parent.
blocks.reasoning: Function props enable child-to-parent communication for events.

blocks.question: BUG FIX: You wrote <LessonCard title="React" /> but inside component you wrote props.Title with capital T. What happens?
options: It works fine, React ignores case
It shows undefined / empty because props.title!= props.Title - case sensitive
App crashes completely
Props automatically convert to lowercase
blocks.correctFeedback: Yes! Case sensitive bug - most common props bug. title vs Title are different props.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Props are case-sensitive like JavaScript variables. title!= Title. Always match spelling exactly.
blocks.reasoning: Understanding case sensitivity prevents common props bugs.

blocks.text: PAGE 12: Towards Your Final Target - How Props Build Lesson 10 App
Let's connect dots to your target: Lesson 10 says Build Complete React Application combining components, JSX, props, state, hooks, routing. Today you mastered props - the glue.

Your dashboard you built: hero uses CourseIcon + Badge + ProgressBar (composition). LessonGrid maps lessons array and renders LessonCard with props (id, title, learn, status, summary). LessonCard receives status prop and shows different badge color + button text (conditional rendering with props). When user clicks Start, LessonCard calls onStart function prop to navigate (child to parent communication). That's props everywhere!
In Lesson 4, we will make status dynamic with state - when user completes Lesson 2, status prop changes from locked to current automatically. Props + State = Magic.

You mastered: Props = arguments for components, passing multiple props, destructuring {id, title}, default props {status='locked'}, children prop for wrappers, props are read-only, rendering lists with map + props + key, prop drilling chain, and function as prop for child-to-parent talk. blocks.question: FINAL APPLICATION: Your boss says: 'We have 50 lessons now, not 10. Dashboard must show all 50 without copying code.' What do you do?
options: Copy paste LessonCard 50 times and manually change titles
Keep ONE LessonCard component with props, put 50 lesson objects in lessons array, use lessons.map(lesson => <LessonCard key={lesson.id} {...lesson} />) - automatically shows 50 cards
Create 50 different files: LessonCard1.jsx to LessonCard50.jsx
Props cannot handle 50 items
blocks.correctFeedback: BINGO! That's the power of props + map - scale from 10 to 50 to 1000 lessons with zero extra component code. You are now thinking like a senior React dev!
blocks.incorrectFeedback: One component + props + map = infinite scalability. Data drives UI. Add more objects to array, UI auto updates.
blocks.reasoning: Props enable scalable, data-driven UI architecture - core for final Lesson 10 target.
